extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, designers, proofreaders, production staff, and publishers preparing illustrations, tables, and electronic enhancements for publication
extracted.subtask_short: preparing illustrations and tables for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, submitting, numbering, captioning, crediting, and testing illustrations and tables for print and electronic publication, including accessibility and production workflows. Intended to be used by authors and editorial/production teams to ensure reproducible, correctly placed, and properly attributed artwork and tabular material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation for testing electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should have a master checklist in place for each publication format; thorough testing of a web-based publication or app should involve checking it against various documents that describe its intended functionality, behavior, and navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists usually suffice for e-book formats and for journal workflows that produce PDF or full-text HTML. For web/apps, testing should use feature-definition documents (detailed feature behavior), use-case documents (step-by-step user interactions), wireframes/design mockups (visual layout), user-interface specifications, and test-case documents (step-by-step testing instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating changes across different formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an augmented PDF for proofreading and maintain an error-reporting system for each electronic format tested in situ; the location of each reported error in each format should be made clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors mark changes on PDFs; use searchable phrases or page-number references. For web/app production, follow an elaborate, flexible system (centralized database) for tracking and implementing changes and stylistic decisions. Procedures should be fully documented with input from developers, designers, editors, proofreaders, and testers. Database entries plus testing documentation can serve as a contract between editors and production to ensure each change is implemented properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations (figures, artwork) are images presented separately from the run of text and usually consist of individual electronic files optimized for specific publication formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations can include paintings, photographs, line drawings, maps, charts, musical-score examples, and multimedia for electronic formats. See extended discussion for preparation, placement, numbering, and captioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables defined
rubrics_metrics.description: A table is an array of vertical columns and horizontal rows presenting data separately from the run of text and is generally typeset along with text rather than produced as an image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat tables as visual representations of data but composed of alphanumeric text. Follow guidance for preparation, placement, numbering, and editing for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous-tone versus halftone handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous-tone images (paintings, photographs) contain gradations and must be converted to halftone dot patterns for offset printing; color images for screen are in RGB and must be converted to CMYK for print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult publisher guidelines for preparing digital artwork; understand reproduction differences between black-and-white and color printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line art preparation and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Line art consists of solid black on white with no gray screens; charts are usually line art and may be published in black-and-white or color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure line art is properly prepared—consider treatment of shading, labels, and fonts. Publishers can often reproduce computer-generated line art without remaking it if properly prepared; consult publisher instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text figures, plates, and galleries distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Text figures are illustrations interspersed in text; plates are full-page illustrations often printed separately and gathered into galleries; a gallery is a section devoted to illustrations and (if on different stock) is often unpaginated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galleries begin on a recto page and must fall between signatures; page-counts usually divisible by four. If gallery printed with text, pages may be included in numbering even if numbers not printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions, legends, keys, and labels definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption is explanatory text appearing with an illustration (usually below); a key/legend appears within the illustration and identifies symbols; labels are descriptive text within an illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caption used for both brief phrasal title and longer explanatory sentence(s). Keys must be within the figure; labels and lettered parts are described in captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of illustrations relative to text
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should appear as soon as possible after the first text reference to them; in electronic works a captioned thumbnail may appear after the paragraph referencing the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In print the image may precede the reference only if on the same page/two-page spread or if text is too short. Authors/editors must provide placement callouts in the manuscript (callouts are production instructions and not for readers). In electronic markup, callouts point to specific source files. Most illustrations appear at top or bottom of a page; placement may vary in reflowable formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meaning of callouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Callouts (e.g., 'fig. 5 about here') are instructions for typesetting or production and will not appear in the published work; they indicate preferred manuscript placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include callouts for interspersed illustrations; they are unnecessary for gallery illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text references to numbered illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: When many illustrations exist, refer to them by number in text: 'figure 1' or 'fig.' in parenthetical references; never use placement-dependent phrasing like 'the photograph opposite' or 'the graph on this page.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In text 'figure' is set in roman, lowercased, spelled out except in parenthetical references where 'fig.' may be used. Some publications may capitalize; adopt journal/book style. 'Plate' should not be abbreviated to 'pl.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent numbering across print and electronic versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations in works published in both print and electronic versions should be numbered according to the same system and use the same numbers in both versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If electronic version contains extra figures, print references must note availability (e.g., 'available online'). For double numeration or galleries see other rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous versus separate numbering of illustration categories
rubrics_metrics.description: All types of illustrations may be numbered in one continuous sequence, but specific categories (e.g., maps) or different media (e.g., video) may be numbered separately for reader convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose numbering that best serves readers; separate sequences required if different media coexist (e.g., 'video 1').

rubrics_metrics.name: Double numeration for chapter-based works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use chapter-based double numeration in heavily illustrated, scientific, or multi-author books: each illustration carries the chapter number followed by the illustration number (e.g., figure 9.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chapter with one illustration still uses double numeration (e.g., 10.1). Appendix figures can use A.1 format, or lettered appendix + number. Double numeration eases editing and locating figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying parts of an illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use arabic numerals for figures; when a figure has several parts, parts may be lettered (A, B, C) and a single caption should key letters to parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to parts as 'fig. 10.7C' (letters usually italicized). Parts may also be described by relative position on the page; maintain relative positions in electronic versions if using positional descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working numbers for unnumbered illustrations during production
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if illustrations will be unnumbered in the final work, during editing and production all illustrations should carry working numbers (in file names, photocopies, callouts) to ensure correct placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working numbers aid handling and prevent misplacement during production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering of gallery illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations gathered in a gallery need not be numbered unless referred to in the text, but should carry working numbers during editing and production; if numbers are required and other text illustrations exist, adopt two sequences (e.g., figure 1... and plate 1...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide numbering strategy appropriate to the work and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting artwork to the publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors preparing electronic illustrations must consult their publisher before submitting files; many publishers require hard copies or PDF along with electronic artwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply a list of software used, any special fonts, and provide scans made per publisher guidelines (preferably by professional graphic arts service). Color scans/photos from lending institutions or professional prepress service are preferred. Check contracts for permission to include color. Internet-obtained images are usually not acceptable unless optimized for print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying artwork for the publisher (file naming and labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit artwork in separate files with descriptive names that accurately identify each file; include these names on corresponding hard copies and numbers corresponding to manuscript callouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original hard-copy artwork must be clearly identified on the back in pencil or with removable labels; avoid ballpoint pens, staples, felt-tip markers. See numbering and caption guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's inventory of artwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should supply a complete list of illustrations noting any to appear in color, sizing restrictions, duplicates/extras, and any outstanding items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works to be published in multiple formats, note format differences in the inventory. Most publishers expect all illustrations to be supplied at manuscript submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher's inventory and checking of artwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should check each incoming illustration against the author's inventory for resolution/file format compliance, damage, numbering, caption correspondence, and permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request replacements for nonconforming files or damaged originals and track missing illustrations. Ensure captions are supplied as a separate file and verify permissions are in order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cropping, scaling, and shading considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should crop digital copies or mark printouts for reframing; compute finished dimensions from the original to preserve legibility of labels and line weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale images to intended size and print/proof. Avoid hairline rules (may disappear when printed) and avoid shading/color that prints poorly when reduced—use stripes/spots/black-and-white fill patterns in charts. Check publisher acceptance of shading/color in properly prepared line art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher redrawing or correction of artwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may redraw or correct submitted line art if agreed; authors should mark labels to be altered on photocopies or supply a keyed list of many changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent wording, abbreviations, and symbols with the text. Provide separate alphabetical lists of map names when maps are to be redrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption format and punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A caption may be a word/phrase, incomplete sentence, or full sentences; no punctuation is needed after an incomplete-sentence caption, but full sentences require closing punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If most captions are full sentences, incomplete captions may be followed by a period for consistency. Capitalize captions in sentence style; formal titles in captions follow headline style (see chapter 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal titles and typography in captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal titles of works included in captions should follow the rules for titles (headline style, italics or quotation marks as appropriate); titles in other languages follow language-specific rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply chapter 8 title rules for capitalization and italics. Generic titles usually are not capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating illustration numbers from captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustration numbers should be distinct from captions they introduce; a period after the number is usual and authors should use this format in preparing captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other typographic treatments may be used in published versions; extra space may be added between number and caption. Whether 'figure' is spelled out or abbreviated may be specified by journal or chosen by designer/editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using locators and positional descriptors in captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize locators such as top, bottom, left, right, above, below, left to right, clockwise from left, inset when identifying elements within a figure or parts of a composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the term precedes the element it identifies, follow it with a comma or colon if a list follows; in midsentence or following the element, the locator may appear in parentheses. Use similar treatment for lettered parts (usually italicized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying symbols or patterns used in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: When symbols or patterns are used in a map or chart, they must be identified either in a key within the figure or in the caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure keys or caption identify symbols/patterns; see examples for charts and graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying electronic enhancements in captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions to illustrations published in both print and electronic versions should indicate in the print version any electronic enhancement (color, video) available online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the electronic version, specify which features are not available in print (e.g., list under 'Enhancements' or 'Electronic Supplements').

rubrics_metrics.name: Including original dimensions and magnification in captions
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving dimensions of original artworks, list dimensions after the medium in order height × width × (depth); photomicrographs should include magnification information where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dimensions only if relevant to the text or requested by rights holder. Examples: 'Oil on canvas, 45 x 38 cm'; photomicrograph: 'original magnification, x400; bar, 100 μm.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration captions and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To provide accessible content, publishers should consider adding appropriate text alternatives for illustrations in electronic formats; well-marked captions and alt text will help text-to-speech and related tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/authors should decide whether an illustration needs alt text and how to write it, consulting DIAGRAM Center, WAI, and EPUB accessibility guidelines. Proper markup enhances accessibility for people with disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit lines: sources, permissions, and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A credit line is a brief statement of the source of an illustration; illustrative material under copyright usually requires permission from the copyright owner before reproduction; authors must consult publishers about permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain written permission and, if required, a print of the work; do not reproduce identifiable human subjects without consent/model release. See chapters on permissions. Credit lines should include author, title, publication details, page/figure numbers as needed; shortened forms may be used if listed in bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and format of credit lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit lines usually appear at the end of a caption, sometimes in parentheses or in different type; in heavily illustrated works credits may be listed together in back matter if permissions allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some permission-grantors stipulate the exact credit-line placement or language and may charge different fees depending on placement; editors should exercise discretion to follow the spirit of required wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting author-supplied, commissioned, free, and public-domain material
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-created illustrations need no credit lines but may use 'Photo by author' for consistency; commissioned work is usually credited (e.g., 'Map by Kevin Hand'); material obtained free may be credited 'courtesy of'; public-domain illustrations may be reproduced without permission but credit lines are appropriate for readers' information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect contractual arrangements (work made for hire) and professional courtesy. Creative Commons or similar licenses may permit reproduction—note licensing in credits as required.
